primitives.name: Free-First Sourcing Priority Rule
primitives.verbatim_quote: ## Spend guard Before any paid API call, the pipeline asks `paidCallJustified(need, sport)` / `requiresPaidEscalation(need, sport)`.
primitives.latex: \text{If } S_{\text{free}} \cap S_{\text{cleared}} \neq \emptyset \text{ then } p^* = \arg\min_{p \in S_{\text{free}} \cap S_{\text{cleared}}} C(p)
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'C(p)': 'Cost of data source $p$', 'S_{\\text{free}}': 'Set of all free data sources', 'S_{\\text{cleared}}': 'Set of all cleared data sources'}
primitives.assumptions: (1) Rights/clearance is a hard constraint; (2) Quality is monotonically related to cost; (3) No source is universally superior across all needs.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Applies when multiple free sources overlap; fails when all free sources are gated or of inferior quality.

layer2.mapping: Maps to GSI's `requiresPaidEscalation` function, which performs a binary check on whether a need requires paid escalation based on the existence of a cleared free alternative. It also mirrors GSE's routing logic that prioritizes free sources over paid ones.
layer2.telemetry: Ratio of free vs. paid API calls per period, weighted by data quality metrics.

The core challenge is balancing budget constraints (tight money) with the imperative for high-quality statistical data (king of stats). The 'Free-First' rule formalizes this as a constrained optimization problem: minimize cost while ensuring the selected source meets both clearance and quality thresholds. Mathematically, this is a set intersection operation followed by a cost minimization over the feasible region. The rule explicitly states that cost cannot override legal/rights clearance, which introduces a hard inequality constraint (C(p) > C_{\text{licensed}}) that must be satisfied before any paid source can be considered. Furthermore, among sources that pass the clearance filter, the rule selects the highest-quality one, implying an implicit utility or quality metric Q(p) that is maximized subject to the cost and clearance constraints. This structure prevents "cheap" fake data from being dressed up as fresh, enforcing the `noFakeLiveData` invariant. The rule also inherently supports scalability by creating a clear hierarchy for adapter development (step 2) and trial management (step 5), thus decoupling short-term operational costs from long-term infrastructure investment.
